title: Primary math foundations
description: Grade 2–3 number sense, operations and fractions, learned by explaining and checking — no code required.
assumptions: Learner can count to 100 and recognizes the + and − symbols. No multiplication or fraction background is assumed.
stage.1.title: Number sense and checking
stage.1.goal: Read three-digit numbers by place, match operations to stories, and verify subtraction with addition.
stage.2.title: Equal groups and fractions
stage.2.goal: Read multiplication as equal groups, name fractions from equal parts, and solve stories with a reasonableness check.
place-value.title: Place value: digits have jobs
place-value.goal: Read and write three-digit numbers by the job of each digit.
place-value.reading: In 352, the 3 is in the hundreds place, the 5 in the tens place, and the 2 in the ones place. So 352 = 300 + 50 + 2. The same digit 5 means different amounts in 52 and 352: in 52 it is 5 tens (50); in 352 it is also 5 tens, but in 502 it would be 5 hundreds (500). Always ask: which place is the digit standing in?
place-value.exercise: Write three numbers that contain the digit 5 in different places. For each, say aloud what the 5 is worth. Then swap two digits in one number and explain how the amount changed.
place-value.rubric: You can point to each digit, name its place, and say its value in ones. You explain why 502 and 352 are different even though they use the same digits.
place-value.q1.q: In the number 352, what does the digit 5 stand for?
place-value.q1.a.fb: The 5 is not in the ones place; the 2 is. Look at which place the 5 stands in.
place-value.q1.b.fb: Right: the 5 stands in the tens place, so it is worth 50.
place-value.q1.c.fb: The hundreds place holds the 3. The 5 is one place to its right.
place-value.q1.hint.1: Count the places from the right: ones, tens, hundreds.
add-meaning.title: Addition means joining
add-meaning.goal: Match addition to stories that join two amounts into one total.
add-meaning.reading: Addition joins amounts. "24 apples and 18 more apples" joins two groups, so 24 + 18 fits. "24 apples and eat 18" takes away, so it fits subtraction, not addition. Before computing, say the story in your own words and decide: are we joining, or taking apart?
add-meaning.exercise: Write one joining story for 35 + 27 using things at home. Draw or act it out, then say why addition is the right operation.
add-meaning.rubric: Your story clearly joins two groups into a total, and you can explain why adding matches the story instead of subtracting.
add-meaning.q1.a: 24 apples, then 18 more apples are put in the basket.
add-meaning.q1.a.fb: Right: two groups are joined, so addition fits.
add-meaning.q1.b.fb: Eating takes away; that story fits 24 − 18, not addition.
add-meaning.q1.hint.1: Ask: does the story join groups or take away?
subtract-check.title: Subtraction and checking with addition
subtract-check.goal: Subtract two-digit numbers and verify the answer with addition.
subtract-check.reading: Subtraction takes apart: 53 − 27 asks what remains when 27 is taken from 53. Addition and subtraction are partners: if 53 − 27 = 26, then 26 + 27 must return to 53. Checking is not redoing the same subtraction; it is using the partner operation to test the answer.
subtract-check.exercise: Compute 62 − 38, then check with addition. Write both number sentences and explain in one sentence why the check proves the answer.
subtract-check.rubric: You compute the difference, write the matching addition check, and explain that the check returns to the starting amount.
subtract-check.q1.a.fb: This adds the starting amount and the taken-away amount; it does not return to the start from the answer.
subtract-check.q1.b.fb: Right: answer plus taken-away amount returns to the starting amount.
subtract-check.q1.hint.1: The check starts from your answer, not from 53.
multiply-meaning.title: Multiplication means equal groups
multiply-meaning.goal: Read multiplication as equal groups and connect it to repeated addition.
multiply-meaning.reading: 4 × 3 means 4 groups of 3: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. The groups must be equal. "4 plates with 3 cookies each" fits 4 × 3; "4 cookies and 3 more cookies" is joining unequal groups and fits 4 + 3. Say "groups of" aloud before you compute.
multiply-meaning.exercise: Find two equal-group situations at home (tiles, eggs, chairs). Write each as "groups of", as repeated addition, and as multiplication.
multiply-meaning.rubric: You identify equal groups, write the repeated addition, and match the multiplication sentence to the groups.
multiply-meaning.q1.a.fb: Right: four equal groups, each holding 3.
multiply-meaning.q1.b.fb: Joining 4 and 3 is 4 + 3; multiplication needs equal groups.
multiply-meaning.q1.hint.1: Say it aloud: four groups of three.
fraction-intuition.title: Fractions are equal parts of one whole
fraction-intuition.goal: Recognize simple fractions as equal parts of one whole.
fraction-intuition.reading: One half means one of two EQUAL parts of one whole. If a pizza is cut into two pieces of different sizes, one piece is not one half. One third means one of three equal parts. The bottom number counts the equal parts; the top number counts how many you take.
fraction-intuition.exercise: Fold a paper strip into 2 equal parts, then another into 4 equal parts. Shade one part of each and say the fraction. Explain why equal parts matter.
fraction-intuition.rubric: You name the fraction from equal parts and explain why unequal pieces cannot be named with the same fraction.
fraction-intuition.q1.a: A circle cut into two pieces, one much bigger than the other.
fraction-intuition.q1.a.fb: The parts are not equal, so one piece is not one half.
fraction-intuition.q1.b: A circle cut into two equal pieces, one shaded.
fraction-intuition.q1.b.fb: Right: one of two equal parts is one half.
fraction-intuition.q1.hint.1: Check the word EQUAL before naming the fraction.
word-problems.title: Choose the operation, then check the answer
word-problems.goal: Solve one-step and two-step stories by choosing the operation and checking reasonableness.
word-problems.reading: Read the story twice. First decide what happens: joining (add), taking away (subtract), equal groups (multiply), or sharing into equal groups (divide). "24 students, 6 at each table, how many tables?" shares 24 into groups of 6, so 24 ÷ 6 = 4 tables. After computing, ask: does 4 tables make sense for 24 students? An answer bigger than the whole class would not.
word-problems.exercise: Write your own table-sharing story with different numbers. Solve it, then check the answer by multiplying back. Trade stories with someone and check each other.
word-problems.rubric: You choose the operation from the story, compute, and check reasonableness with the partner operation.
word-problems.q1.q: 24 students sit 6 at each table. Which number sentence finds the tables?
word-problems.q1.a.fb: Right: sharing 24 into equal groups of 6 gives the number of tables.
word-problems.q1.b.fb: Multiplying would make 144 students, more than the whole class; the answer would not make sense.
word-problems.q1.hint.1: Are we making equal groups from a total? That is division.
multiply-meaning.struggle: Before reading: use 12 small objects to show what 4 × 3 could mean. Arrange them, draw your arrangement, and write why it fits 4 × 3. There may be more than one right arrangement, or a wrong one; keep your first try.
fraction-intuition.struggle: Before reading: draw two circles. Cut one into two equal parts and shade one; cut the other into two unequal parts and shade one. Write which shaded piece is one half and how you know. Keep your first answer even if unsure.
fraction-intuition.s1.content: Cut one circle into 2 EQUAL parts and shade 1 part. The shaded part is one half of the circle, written 1/2.
fraction-intuition.s1.prompt: In your own words: why must the parts be equal? What happens if they are not?
fraction-intuition.s1.fb: Exactly — a fraction names equal parts; unequal pieces cannot share one fraction name.
fraction-intuition.s1.hint: Imagine one piece much bigger than the other.
fraction-intuition.s2.prompt: A circle is cut into 4 equal parts and 1 is shaded. What is the denominator of the fraction?
fraction-intuition.s2.fb: Right: the denominator counts the total equal parts, which is 4.
fraction-intuition.s2.hint: The denominator counts all the equal parts.
fraction-intuition.s3.fb: Correct: one of two equal parts is one half.
fraction-intuition.s3.a: A circle in two unequal pieces, one shaded.
fraction-intuition.s3.a.fb: The parts are unequal, so one piece is not one half.
fraction-intuition.s3.b: A circle in two equal pieces, one shaded.
fraction-intuition.s3.b.fb: Yes: one of two equal parts.
fraction-intuition.s4.prompt: Put the steps for showing one third in order.
fraction-intuition.s4.fb: Right: divide into equal parts first, take one part, then write the fraction.
fraction-intuition.s4.cut: Divide one whole into 3 equal parts.
fraction-intuition.s4.hint: You must divide before you can take a part.
fraction-intuition.denominator.scaffold: The denominator is not the shaded parts — it is the total number of equal parts the whole is cut into. Count all the equal parts first, then look at how many are shaded.
